subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 14 periods = 560 minutes
Total: 14 periods · 9h 20min

section_titles: Comparing lengths using informal tools
periods.activity_title: Party Measures: Whose Hand Span Wins?

tasks_in_class.description: Discuss and explain what various activities are shown in the party picture.
Discuss how Shelly finds the height of the door.
Will Leena and Adi get the same measurement of the table using their hand spans? Discuss.
Circle the child with the longest ponytail.

time_bands.activity: Open the party picture together. Let us Do Q1, p.128 ("discuss what various activities are shown....") — children name what each person is doing to measure something, in their own words.

Let us Do Q2, p.128 ("discuss how Shelly finds the height of the door....") — children mime using hand spans up a wall, then Let us Do Q3, p.128 ("will Leena and Adi get the same measurement....") — pairs place their hand spans side by side to feel the difference.
Children actually span the desk or a book with their own hands and record a count; two or three volunteers share their counts and notice they differ. The class discusses why.
Let us Do Q4, p.128 ("circle the child with the longest ponytail....") — children look closely at the picture and circle their answer, then explain to a partner how they decided.

periods.teacher_notes: The central idea of this unit is that informal units (hand spans, footsteps) give different results because they vary from person to person — this is the problem the chapter is built to solve. Watch for children who assume everyone's hand span is the same; prompt them to compare their own span with a neighbour's before measuring. Additional practice with the same reasoning: Let us Do Q5–Q7, p.128.
materials: Rulers or desks as surfaces to span

section_titles: Comparing lengths using informal tools
periods.activity_title: Paper Strings on the Board: Shortest to Longest

tasks_in_class.description: Colour the shortest paper string red and the longest green; discuss how you identified each.
How many more paper strings are needed to decorate the border of the green board?
How many of the given unit-string are needed to decorate the entire border of the board?

time_bands.activity: Display several strips of coloured paper of different lengths across the board or a string line. Children look without touching and predict which is shortest and longest.

Let us Do Q1, p.129 ("colour the shortest paper string red and the longest green....") — children colour, then explain to a partner the strategy they used (direct visual comparison, lining up one end).
Let us Do Q2, p.129 ("how many more paper strings are needed to decorate the border....") — children count along the picture border and work out the difference.

Let us Do Q3, p.129 ("how many of the given unit-string are needed to decorate the entire border....") — children use the unit string as a repeated measure around the board border and arrive at a count.

periods.teacher_notes: Building on the idea that lengths can vary, this unit shifts to comparing and counting lengths visually and with a unit string. A common error is children counting corners of the border as separate units; guide them to lay the unit string continuously without gaps or overlaps. T-5 and T-6 (measuring the window height and the wall distance) work well as extension tasks if the class finishes early.
materials: Coloured paper strips of varying lengths (pre-cut, 5–6 strips)

section_titles: Drawing and comparing lengths

tasks_in_class.description: Cut and paste a wool or cotton thread as long as the line given below.
Draw a string longer than the string given below.
Draw a string shorter than the decoration string Shelly and Adi are holding.
Draw the other half of the moustache to match the given half.
Look at the string lights and help Adi choose the longest one; discuss how you found out.

time_bands.activity: Distribute wool or thread and scissors. Let us Do Q1, p.130 ("cut and paste a wool or cotton thread as long as the line....") — children place thread along the printed line, cut, and paste. The physical act of matching sets up the idea of reproducing a length.

Let us Do Q2, p.130 ("draw a string longer than the string given....") and Let us Do Q3, p.130 ("draw a string shorter than the decoration string....") — children draw their own lines, then hold their books next to the given strings to verify.
Let us Do Q4, p.130 ("draw the other half of the moustache to match the given half....") — children fold the page lightly to see where the mirror line falls, then draw the missing half freehand.

Let us Do Q5, p.130 ("look at the string lights and help Adi choose the longest....") — children discuss in pairs, share their reasoning, and agree on a strategy for comparing curvy or looped strings.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit moves from observing lengths to physically reproducing and drawing them. For T-14, children often draw the moustache half at a wrong angle rather than as a mirror reflection; ask them to fold the page along the centre line and hold it up to the light to check. T-12 and T-13 are distinct acts (longer vs. shorter) rather than duplicates, so both are kept in class.
materials: Wool or cotton thread (one length per child)

section_titles: Indirect measurement with a common unit
periods.activity_title: Bridge Test: Does the Table Fit Through the Door?

tasks_in_class.description: Make a bridge using boxes or bags; guess and check which classroom objects can go through it.

time_bands.activity: Read the textbook story of Shelly and Adi checking whether the table fits through the door. Ask: how could you find out without moving the table to the door? Collect ideas; introduce the thread-as-go-between approach.

Demonstrate with a thread: stretch it across the table's width, keep that length, carry it to the door gap, and compare. Children watch and then name what the thread is doing (acting as a common measure between two objects that cannot be placed side by side).

Let us Play, p.132 ("make a bridge using boxes or bags; guess and check which objects can go through....") — groups of four build their bridge gap from two stacks of books or bags, guess which items fit, then use a thread to check before physically testing.
Each group shares one surprising result — an object they thought would fit but did not, or vice versa. The class discusses why the thread method is more reliable than guessing by eye.

periods.teacher_notes: The key idea this unit develops is indirect comparison: measuring one object with a thread and using that thread to compare with a second object, without the two objects ever touching. Watch for children who simply hold the two objects up next to each other instead of using the thread; redirect them to the specific challenge of comparing without direct contact. The textbook context (table and door) makes the need for indirect comparison genuinely motivating.
materials: Lengths of string or wool (one per group)
Books or bags to make bridge gaps
Assorted classroom objects of varied widths (pencil case, book, lunch box)

section_titles: Body measurement exploration
periods.activity_title: True or False? Checking Body Proportion Claims

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Are these true for all? Q1, p.133
tasks_in_class.description: Measure and tick: Is your head 3 handspans round? True or False.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Are these true for all? Q2, p.133
tasks_in_class.description: Measure and tick: Is the length of your forearm equal to the length of your feet? True or False.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Are these true for all? Q3, p.133
tasks_in_class.description: Measure and tick: Is your height equal to the length of your arms wide open? True or False.

time_bands.activity: Announce the three claims written on the board: head round = three hand spans; forearm = foot length; height = arm span wide open. Children vote by show of hands: true or false? Record the class prediction.

Are these true for all? Q1, p.133 ("is your head 3 handspans round?") and Q2, p.133 ("is your forearm equal to your foot length?") — pairs measure each other using a thread for the head circumference and by direct comparison for forearm and foot, recording true/false for each person.

Are these true for all? Q3, p.133 ("is your height equal to your arms wide open?") — one child stands against the wall with arms spread; a partner marks both measurements with a thread and compares them. Record and tick in the book.

Class tally: how many found each claim true? How many found it false? Discuss — if the same claim is sometimes true and sometimes false for different children, what does that tell us about using body parts as measurement units?

periods.teacher_notes: This unit is designed to surface the core limitation of body-based informal units through personal data: because children get different answers, the class itself generates the evidence for why a unit that does not vary from person to person is needed. Watch for children who mark 'true' without actually measuring; insist on the thread-and-compare step before ticking. All three tasks develop distinct claims, so all are kept in class.
materials: Thread or wool cut to manageable lengths (one per pair)

section_titles: Introducing the metre as a standard unit
periods.activity_title: Making and Folding the One-Metre Rope

tasks_in_class.description: Measure your height using the one-metre mark on the wall; record friends' names as more or less than one metre.
Circle the tallest among the children shown and discuss how you decided.
Write names of objects around you whose length is one metre, more than one metre, and less than one metre.

time_bands.activity: Use a metre rod to mark exactly one metre on the wall (tape or chalk mark). Children take turns standing against the mark; the class decides whether each child is more than, equal to, or less than one metre tall. Measure your height activity, p.135 ("record friends' names as more or less than one metre...."): record names in the two columns.

Circle the tallest activity, p.135 ("circle the tallest among the children shown and discuss how you decided....") — children compare the pictured heights and explain their reasoning, including how the one-metre line in the picture helps.
Children take a one-metre rope and fold it once (half metre) and again (quarter metre); mark the folds with a twist of tape. Introduce the names half metre and quarter metre at the fold points.

Objects table activity, p.136 ("write names of objects whose length is one metre, more than one metre, and less than one metre....") — children look around the room and write two objects in each column.

periods.teacher_notes: The metre is introduced here as a shared, person-independent unit — in direct contrast to the hand spans and body measurements explored earlier. The act of folding the rope is the students' first encounter with half metre and quarter metre as derived subdivisions; ensure each child makes and labels their own folded rope as they will use it in the unit that follows. A common error is children confusing 'more than one metre tall' with 'exactly one metre' — use the wall mark as a clear reference.
materials: Metre rod or measured tape (for wall marking)
Rope or thick string cut to exactly one metre per child

section_titles: Measuring with metre, half metre, and quarter metre
periods.activity_title: Measure Everything: Metre, Half, Quarter Ropes at Work

tasks_in_class.description: Find lengths of different objects using one metre, half metre, and quarter metre ropes; fill the table.
Draw a start line and a one-metre line; jump and record which children jump more than a quarter, half, and a full metre.
Throw a ball or disc as far as you can; measure how far the throw was.

time_bands.activity: Let us Do Q1, p.137 ("find lengths of different objects using one metre, half metre, and quarter metre ropes; fill the table....") — small groups rotate among five objects, choosing the appropriate rope and recording the category in the table.

Move to a clear floor space. Let us Do Q2, p.137 ("draw a start line and a one-metre line; jump and record....") — children take turns jumping from the start line; others place the quarter-, half-, and full-metre ropes to decide which band the jump lands in.

Let us Do Q3, p.137 ("throw a ball or disc as far as you can; measure how far the throw was....") — pairs throw and place the rope to measure; one or two results are shared and compared to the jump distances to build a sense of how the unit scales.

periods.teacher_notes: Children have met the metre, half metre, and quarter metre as folded rope subdivisions; this unit asks them to use those three ropes as practical measuring tools for the first time. A common error is placing the rope with a gap at the start or overlap at the end; model a flush-end start before groups begin. T-23, T-24, and T-25 each apply the ropes in a different physical context (tabletop objects, floor jump, throw), so all three are kept in class.
materials: One metre, half metre, and quarter metre ropes per group (from folded ropes)
A soft ball or flat disc for throwing
Chalk or tape for floor lines

section_titles: Measuring with metre, half metre, and quarter metre
periods.activity_title: Estimate, Cut, Count: Sharpening Metre Sense

tasks_in_class.description: Measure the height of your teacher or parent using a metre-long rope or strip.
Estimate and cut a one-metre long wool or thread; verify with the metre rope whose estimate is closest.
Cut a one-metre rope into 4 equal pieces. How many cuts did you make?
How many footsteps fit into a metre rope?
Use a metre rope to find how long a side of the class wall is.

time_bands.activity: Let us Do Q1, p.138 ("measure the height of your teacher or parent using a metre-long rope or strip....") — the teacher stands against the wall; children place the metre rope repeatedly to count how many metres (and part-metres) tall the teacher is. Record the result.

Let us Do Q2, p.138 ("estimate and cut a one-metre long wool; verify with the metre rope whose estimate is closest....") — each child tears or cuts a length of wool by eye without measuring, then holds it beside the metre rope to see the difference. The class finds whose cut is closest.
Let us Do Q3, p.138 ("cut a one-metre rope into 4 equal pieces; how many cuts?") — children fold and cut, then count the cuts and discuss: four equal pieces need only three cuts, not four.

Let us Do Q4, p.138 ("how many footsteps fit into a metre rope?") — children lay the rope on the floor and count their own footsteps across it; compare counts. Then Let us Do Q5, p.138 ("use a metre rope to find how long a side of the class wall is....") — children place and count the rope lengths along one wall.

periods.teacher_notes: The estimate-and-verify cycle in T-27 is the heart of this unit: children build an internal sense of one metre by committing to a cut before measuring. A common error in T-28 is children saying 'four pieces, so four cuts' — the folding step makes the three-cut answer visible before scissors are used. T-29 and T-30 extend the metre as a repeated unit, directly connecting back to the counting-unit-strings work from the paper-border tasks.
materials: Wool or thick thread for estimating and cutting
Chalk or tape for wall measurement

section_titles: Comparing lengths using informal tools
periods.activity_title: Measure the Room: Class Survey with Informal Units

tasks_in_class.description: Tick paper strings in the classroom that are as long as the height of the window.
Find the distance between two walls of the classroom and discuss different ways of measuring it.
Identify all ways children use to measure length in the picture; which way is better and why?

time_bands.activity: Post several paper strings of different lengths around the room (door, window frame, board edge). Let us Do Q5, p.128 ("tick paper strings that are as long as the height of the window....") — children walk around, hold each string against the window height, and tick their book.

Let us Do Q6, p.128 ("find the distance between two walls; discuss different ways of measuring it....") — small groups each choose a different method (footsteps, hand spans, a string) and measure the same wall-to-wall distance, then share results on the board.

Let us Do Q7, p.128 ("identify all ways children use to measure length; which way is better and why?") — using the board data from the previous activity, children discuss why different methods gave different numbers, and vote on which approach was most consistent.

periods.teacher_notes: The class survey in this unit produces a natural data set: different methods give different answers for the same wall-to-wall distance, making the inconsistency of informal units concrete and personal. Steer the closing discussion toward the idea that a method is 'better' when everyone using it gets the same answer — this prepares the conceptual ground for the standard metre. Watch for groups who rush through measuring without recording their count.
materials: Pre-cut paper strings of 4–6 different lengths posted around the room
Chalk or whiteboard space for recording group results

section_titles: Drawing and comparing lengths
Indirect measurement with a common unit

tasks_in_class.description: Look at the string lights and help Adi choose the longest one; discuss how you found out.
Make a bridge using boxes or bags; guess and check which classroom objects can go through it.

time_bands.activity: Let us Do Q5, p.130 ("look at the string lights and help Adi choose the longest one; discuss how you found out....") — children study the picture, choose the longest string light, and articulate their comparison strategy to the class; the teacher records the different strategies.

Introduce the indirect-measurement problem from the textbook (p.132): how do Shelly and Adi check whether the table fits through the door without moving it? Children suggest ideas; demonstrate the thread-carry method.

Let us Play, p.132 ("make a bridge using boxes or bags; guess and check which objects can go through it....") — groups build a gap, guess which items clear it, then use a thread to verify before physically testing.
Quick class share: which object most surprised the group — did the thread prediction match the physical test? Children name what the thread is doing in this task.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit brings together two related skills: visual length comparison (string lights) and indirect comparison using a thread as a common intermediary. The bridge activity is designed so children generate their own predictions before measuring, making the verify step meaningful. Watch for children who bypass the thread and directly trial-and-error each object through the bridge — prompt them to use the thread first, then test.
materials: Textbook open to p.130 and p.132
Books or bags to build bridge gaps
Thread or string lengths (one per group)
Assorted classroom objects of varied widths

section_titles: Body measurement exploration
Introducing the metre as a standard unit
periods.activity_title: From Body Units to the Metre: Why We Need One Standard

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Are these true for all? Q1, p.133
tasks_in_class.description: Measure and tick: Is your head 3 handspans round? True or False.
Measure your height using the one-metre mark on the wall; record friends' names as more or less than one metre.
Write names of objects around you whose length is one metre, more than one metre, and less than one metre.

time_bands.activity: Are these true for all? Q1, p.133 ("is your head 3 handspans round? True or False") — pairs use a thread to measure head circumference, then wrap it in hand spans and tick their result. Three or four children share their readings; the class sees that hand span counts differ.

Transition question: if hand spans differ, what kind of unit would give everyone the same answer? Introduce the metre mark on the wall (taped or chalked at exactly one metre). Measure your height activity, p.135 ("record friends' names as more or less than one metre....") — pairs measure and record.

Objects table activity, p.136 ("write names of objects whose length is one metre, more than one metre, and less than one metre....") — children look around the room, identify objects, and fill the three columns. Pairs compare their lists and resolve any disagreements with the metre rope.

periods.teacher_notes: The arc of this unit is deliberate: opening with informal body-unit measurement and immediately following with the metre allows children to feel the contrast in the same sitting. The class data from the head-circumference activity (different hand-span counts for the same head) is the motivation for accepting the metre as a shared standard. Watch for children who conflate 'one metre tall' with 'the tallest in the class' — use the wall mark to clarify.
materials: Thread for head circumference (one length per pair)
Metre mark on the wall (tape or chalk, pre-prepared)
Textbook open to p.133 and p.135–136

section_titles: Measuring with metre, half metre, and quarter metre
periods.activity_title: Jump, Throw, Measure: Standard Units in Action

tasks_in_class.description: Find lengths of different objects using one metre, half metre, and quarter metre ropes; fill the table.
Draw a start line and a one-metre line; jump and record which children jump more than a quarter, half, and a full metre.
Cut a one-metre rope into 4 equal pieces. How many cuts did you make?

time_bands.activity: Let us Do Q1, p.137 ("find lengths of different objects using one metre, half metre, and quarter metre ropes; fill the table....") — groups of three rotate among five pre-placed objects, select the right rope, measure, and record the category in the table.

Move to an open floor area. Let us Do Q2, p.137 ("draw a start line and a one-metre line; jump and record....") — children jump from the chalk start line; classmates place the three ropes to identify the band each jump falls into and record names.
Let us Do Q3, p.138 ("cut a one-metre rope into 4 equal pieces; how many cuts?") — children fold and cut, count the cuts, and explain to a partner why the answer is three and not four.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit gives children a second encounter with the three rope lengths as measuring tools, consolidating the metre subdivisions through physical activity before the estimation tasks in the unit that follows. A common error in the jump activity is children measuring from where they land to the start line rather than from the start line to where they land; model the correct direction explicitly. T-25 (ball throw) is available as an extension if the class completes early.
materials: One metre, half metre, and quarter metre ropes per group
Chalk or tape for floor lines
Five classroom objects of varied lengths (pre-placed)
Scissors and spare rope for Q3

section_titles: Measuring with metre, half metre, and quarter metre
periods.activity_title: Estimate, Verify, and Count: Wall to Wall in Metres

tasks_in_class.description: Measure the height of your teacher or parent using a metre-long rope or strip.
Estimate and cut a one-metre long wool or thread; verify with the metre rope whose estimate is closest.
How many footsteps fit into a metre rope?
Use a metre rope to find how long a side of the class wall is.

time_bands.activity: Let us Do Q1, p.138 ("measure the height of your teacher or parent using a metre-long rope or strip....") — the teacher stands against the wall; children count how many full metre-rope lengths fit and note any remainder. Record on the board.

Let us Do Q2, p.138 ("estimate and cut a one-metre long wool; verify with the metre rope whose estimate is closest....") — each child pulls and cuts a length of wool by eye; all hold cuts beside the metre rope and the class identifies whose estimate is closest. Discuss what strategies helped.

Let us Do Q4, p.138 ("how many footsteps fit into a metre rope?") — children lay the rope on the floor and count their footsteps across it; three volunteers share their counts and note differences, connecting back to the earlier hand-span discussion.

Let us Do Q5, p.138 ("use a metre rope to find how long a side of the class wall is....") — pairs take the rope to one wall, place it end-to-end, count repetitions, and record the result. Pairs compare and resolve any count disagreements.

periods.teacher_notes: The estimate-then-verify cycle in T-27 is a direct application of the measurement sense the chapter has been building; children who have used the metre rope repeatedly in earlier units will have a more calibrated guess. Watch for children who make only a short cut and then stretch it to the metre rope — the estimate must be committed before any checking. T-30 closes S6: all sections are now complete.
materials: Wool or thick thread for estimating

periods.activity_title: From Hand Span to Metre: Our Whole-Chapter Measurement Fair

tasks_in_class.description: Identify all ways children use to measure length in the picture; which way is better and why?
How many of the given unit-string are needed to decorate the entire border of the board?
Make a bridge using boxes or bags; guess and check which classroom objects can go through it.
Estimate and cut a one-metre long wool or thread; verify with the metre rope whose estimate is closest.

time_bands.activity: Open with a quick class survey on the board: children call out one informal unit (hand span, footstep, head circumference) and one standard unit (metre, half metre, quarter metre) they used across this chapter. The teacher lists them in two columns.

Let us Do Q7, p.128 ("identify all ways children use to measure length; which way is better and why?") — children revisit the party picture and explain, using words from the board columns, why informal units give different answers for different people while the metre gives everyone the same answer.

Let us Do Q3, p.129 ("how many of the given unit-string are needed to decorate the entire border of the board?") and Let us Play, p.132 ("make a bridge using boxes or bags; guess and check which objects can go through it....") — half the class solves the border problem while the other half runs the bridge check; groups rotate. Both tasks require choosing a measurement strategy, echoing the chapter's full arc.

Let us Do Q2, p.138 ("estimate and cut a one-metre long wool; verify with the metre rope whose estimate is closest....") — every child cuts a length by eye, holds it to the metre rope, and records how close their estimate was. The class discusses how the metre now feels as a known quantity compared with a hand span or footstep.

Closing conversation: a child names one thing they can measure better now than at the start of the chapter, and explains which tool they would choose and why. The teacher draws the two columns from the opening back into view and asks: what changed between the left column and the right?

periods.teacher_notes: This unit draws together the full journey — from informal units that vary with the person, through indirect comparison with a thread, through body-proportion testing, to the metre as a shared standard — by revisiting representative tasks from each strand. The four tasks span informal comparison (Q7, p.128), unit-counting (Q3, p.129), indirect measurement (bridge, p.132), and standard-unit estimation (Q2, p.138). Choose the closing child speaker deliberately: a student who earlier found the informal-vs-standard contrast surprising will make the reflection most vivid.
materials: Textbook open to p.128, p.129, p.132, p.138
Books or bags for bridge gaps
Chalk or whiteboard for two-column list

items.prompt: Riya measures the length of a table using her hand span. She counts 8 hand spans. Her friend Mona measures the same table and counts 10 hand spans. Which of the following best explains why they got different counts?

options.label: A
options.text: Hand span is a standard unit so both should get the same number.

options.label: B
options.text: Riya and Mona have different-sized hand spans.

options.label: C
options.text: Riya made a counting mistake.

options.label: D
options.text: The table changed size between the two measurements.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: B — Riya and Mona have different-sized hand spans.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: The hand span is an informal, non-standard unit that varies from person to person, so the same length gives different counts for different people.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student thinks measurement differences are always due to counting errors, not unit size variation.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student does not yet understand that the object being measured stays the same; only the measurer changes.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student confuses hand span with a standard unit, not yet grasping that standard means the same for everyone.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student place their hand span beside a partner's to see the size difference directly; stretch: ask what would happen if three more children measured.

exercise.description: Find the distance between two walls of the classroom and discuss different ways of measuring it.

items.prompt: Look at the line below. Draw a new line that is shorter than this line. How do you know your line is shorter?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Any line visibly shorter than the given reference line; the student explains by lining up one end and seeing the new line ends before the given line ends.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Place one end of both lines at the same point and compare where each line ends.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student use a piece of thread to copy the reference line, then cut a shorter piece to draw from; stretch: draw a line shorter than the reference but longer than half of it.

exercise.description: Cut and paste a wool or cotton thread as long as the line given below.

items.prompt: A butterfly picture has one wing drawn. The other wing is missing. The butterfly's wings are equal and mirror each other. Describe what you would do to draw the missing wing so it matches the given wing.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The student describes folding the page along the middle line (the body) to see where the given wing falls, then drawing the missing wing on the other side to match it in shape and length.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Fold along the centre line to find the mirror position, then draw the matching half.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student fold the paper and hold it up to light to trace the outline; stretch: describe two differences that would make the wings not match.

exercise.description: Draw the other half of the moustache to match the given half.

items.section_title: Indirect measurement with a common unit
items.prompt: Priya wants to find out if her school bag fits through a narrow gap between two shelves without moving the shelves or the bag next to each other. What should she do?

options.label: A
options.text: Guess by looking at the gap and the bag.

options.label: B
options.text: Measure the gap with her hand span and the bag with her hand span.

options.label: C
options.text: Push the bag in and see what happens.

options.label: D
options.text: Use a thread to measure the width of the bag, carry the thread to the gap, and compare.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: B — use a thread to measure the bag's width, carry the thread to the gap, and compare.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use a thread as a common intermediary to transfer a measurement from one object to another without placing them side by side.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student relies on visual estimation without a tool, which may work for obvious differences but fails for close lengths.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student uses hand spans, which gives two different counts rather than a direct comparison, missing the indirect-comparison idea.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student skips measurement entirely and uses trial-and-error, which may damage the bag or the shelves.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: demonstrate with a thread and two book stacks in class so the student sees the method before answering; stretch: ask how the student would record the result so someone else could check it.

exercise.description: Make a bridge using boxes or bags; guess and check which classroom objects can go through it.

items.prompt: Three children each measure their own height and compare it with their arm span stretched wide open. Arun finds his height equals his arm span. Divya finds her height is a little more than her arm span. Sona finds her arm span is more than her height. What does this tell us?

options.label: A
options.text: At least one of them measured incorrectly.

options.label: B
options.text: Body proportions vary from person to person, so the claim is not true for everyone.

options.label: C
options.text: Only arm span should be used to measure height.

options.label: D
options.text: The claim 'height equals arm span' is true for all children.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: C — body proportions vary from person to person, so the height-equals-arm-span claim is not true for everyone.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare results across multiple people: if the same claim gives different outcomes, the claim does not hold for all.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student assumes all three measured wrongly rather than accepting that body proportions differ.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student ignores Divya's and Sona's contradicting results and accepts the generalisation anyway.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student misreads the conclusion and suggests replacing one informal unit with another.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: pair the student with a partner to measure both their heights and arm spans and compare; stretch: ask whether using a metre rope instead of arm span would give the same result for all three children, and why.

exercise.book_ref: Are these true for all? Q3, p.133
exercise.description: Measure and tick: Is your height equal to the length of your arms wide open? True or False.

items.section_title: Introducing the metre as a standard unit
items.prompt: A line is marked on the wall exactly one metre above the floor. Kavya stands against the wall and her head reaches above the line. Rohan stands against the wall and his head does not reach the line. Write one sentence each to describe Kavya's height and Rohan's height using the word 'metre'.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Kavya's height is more than one metre. Rohan's height is less than one metre.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare each child's height to the one-metre mark: above the mark means more than one metre; below the mark means less than one metre.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student stand at a metre mark on the wall and feel physically whether they are above or below it; stretch: ask what measuring tool they would use to find out exactly how many metres tall Kavya is.

exercise.description: Measure your height using the one-metre mark on the wall; record friends' names as more or less than one metre.

items.section_title: Introducing the metre as a standard unit
items.prompt: Which of the following objects is most likely to be about one metre long?

options.label: A
options.text: A classroom door width

options.label: B
options.text: A pencil

options.label: C
options.text: A postage stamp

options.label: D
options.text: A school bus

teacher_guide.expected_answer: B — a classroom door width is most likely to be about one metre.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare each object's familiar size to the one-metre rope length used in class: a pencil and a stamp are far shorter; a school bus is far longer.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has not yet built a physical sense of one metre as a length and confuses it with a smaller everyday object.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has no referent for one metre and picks an extremely small object.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student confuses one metre with a much larger length.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student hold a one-metre rope and walk to each candidate object to compare; stretch: name one more object in the classroom that is close to one metre and explain how they know.

exercise.description: Write names of objects around you whose length is one metre, more than one metre, and less than one metre.

items.section_title: Measuring with metre, half metre, and quarter metre
items.prompt: A child uses a one-metre rope to measure the length of a classroom wall and counts 5 full rope lengths. She then uses a half-metre rope and gets 10 lengths for the same wall. Which statement correctly explains this?

options.label: A
options.text: She should always use the metre rope and never the half-metre rope.

options.label: B
options.text: The half-metre rope is less accurate than the metre rope.

options.label: C
options.text: The wall changed size between the two measurements.

options.label: D
options.text: Two half-metre ropes make one metre, so 10 half-metres equals 5 metres.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: B — two half-metre ropes make one metre, so 10 half-metres equals 5 metres — both measurements describe the same wall.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Since a half metre is exactly half of one metre, you need twice as many half-metre lengths to cover the same distance.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student does not understand that different unit sizes give proportionally different counts for the same fixed length.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student confuses a smaller unit with being less accurate rather than understanding that smaller units give larger counts.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student draws an incorrect rule that one unit is always better, missing the idea that all three are valid depending on the object.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: fold a metre rope in half and show that two folds cover one metre; stretch: predict how many quarter-metre lengths would cover the same wall.

exercise.description: Find lengths of different objects using one metre, half metre, and quarter metre ropes; fill the table.

items.section_title: Measuring with metre, half metre, and quarter metre
items.prompt: A child measures the length of a classroom wall with a metre rope. She places the rope end-to-end and counts. The number line below shows her count. Fill in the missing numbers.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Counting in ones along the number line: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: lay out five books end-to-end and count them aloud, pointing to each; stretch: ask how many metre ropes in total would be needed if the wall were twice as long.

exercise.description: Use a metre rope to find how long a side of the class wall is.

items.prompt: Ajay measures the width of a door using his hand span and gets 6 hand spans. Neha measures the same door and gets 8 hand spans. They both measured carefully and did not make any mistakes. Explain why they got different answers.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Ajay and Neha have different-sized hand spans, so the same door width takes more of Neha's hand spans (which are smaller) and fewer of Ajay's (which are larger).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: An informal unit like a hand span is not the same size for everyone; a smaller hand span fits more times across the same length.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student place their own hand span beside a classmate's and count the difference; stretch: ask what would happen if a third child with an even smaller hand span measured the same door.

exercise.description: Will Leena and Adi get the same measurement of the table using their hand spans? Discuss.

items.prompt: Four paper strings hang on a board. String W is the shortest and String Z is the longest. String X is longer than String W but shorter than String Y. If you had to colour the second-longest string blue, which would you colour?

options.label: A
options.text: String W

options.label: B
options.text: String X

options.label: C
options.text: String Y

options.label: D
options.text: String Z

teacher_guide.expected_answer: C — String Y. The order from shortest to longest is W, X, Y, Z; the second-longest is Y.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Order the strings from shortest to longest using the given clues: W < X < Y < Z; the second from the top is Y.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student picks the shortest string, confusing 'second-longest' with 'second-shortest' or 'shortest'.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student identifies the second-shortest rather than the second-longest.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student picks the longest string rather than the one immediately below it.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write the four strings in a vertical line from shortest to longest using arrows; stretch: ask what the order would be if a fifth string were added that is longer than Y but shorter than Z.

exercise.description: Colour the shortest paper string red and the longest green; discuss how you identified each.

items.prompt: A green board has a border made of paper strings. There are already 6 paper strings on the border. The full border needs 10 paper strings. How many more paper strings are needed?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Subtract the number already placed from the total needed: 10 − 6 = 4.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw 10 boxes for the border and shade 6 to show what is already there; count the unshaded boxes; stretch: ask how many strings would be needed if the border had 12 spaces but only 3 strings were already placed.

exercise.description: How many more paper strings are needed to decorate the border of the green board?

items.prompt: Three string lights are hanging. String light P is straight and long. String light Q is looped and appears bunched up. String light R is straight and shorter than P. Adi says String Q is the shortest because it looks small. Do you agree? Explain your answer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: No — a looped string may actually be longer than a straight one; to find the true length you must straighten each string out fully before comparing, or use a thread to trace and compare each one.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Straighten or trace each string with a thread to find its true length before comparing.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the student two pieces of string of the same length, one straight and one looped, and ask which looks longer before straightening both; stretch: describe one way to compare two looped strings without straightening either.

exercise.description: Look at the string lights and help Adi choose the longest one; discuss how you found out.

items.section_title: Introducing the metre as a standard unit
items.prompt: Three children stand in a line. Priya's head is above the one-metre mark on the wall. Tarun's head is exactly at the one-metre mark. Sunil's head is below the one-metre mark. Who is the tallest?

options.label: A
options.text: Priya, because her head is above the one-metre mark.

options.label: B
options.text: Sunil, because he is the shortest.

options.label: C
options.text: Tarun, because he is exactly one metre.

options.label: D
options.text: They are all the same height.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: B — Priya is the tallest because her head is above the one-metre mark, meaning she is more than one metre tall.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the one-metre mark as a common reference: the child whose head is highest above it is tallest.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student confuses 'exactly one metre' with tallest, rather than understanding that above the mark means taller.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student confuses 'shortest' with 'tallest' or misreads 'below the mark'.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student ignores the different positions relative to the mark.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw three stick figures next to a vertical line with one above, one at, and one below a marked point; stretch: ask how you could check whether Priya is more than one and a half metres tall.

exercise.description: Circle the tallest among the children shown and discuss how you decided.

items.section_title: Measuring with metre, half metre, and quarter metre
items.prompt: Renu cuts a length of wool and says it looks about one metre. Her friend checks it with a metre rope and says Renu's piece is longer. What should Renu do to find out exactly how much longer her piece is?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Renu should place her wool piece alongside the metre rope, lining up one end exactly, and look at how much of her piece extends beyond the end of the metre rope.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Align one end of the piece with one end of the metre rope and observe the overhang beyond the rope's end.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the student a metre rope and a slightly longer piece of thread to try the comparison physically; stretch: ask how Renu could use a half-metre rope to describe how much longer her piece is.

exercise.description: Estimate and cut a one-metre long wool or thread; verify with the metre rope whose estimate is closest.

items.prompt: The line below is 6 cm long. Which of the following correctly describes a line that is longer than this line?

options.label: A
options.text: A line that is 3 cm long.

options.label: B
options.text: A line that is 4 cm long.

options.label: C
options.text: A line that is 6 cm long.

options.label: D
options.text: A line that is 9 cm long.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: C — a line that is 9 cm long is longer than 6 cm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare the numbers: any length greater than 6 cm is longer than the given line.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student picks a shorter length, confusing 'longer' with 'shorter'.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student picks an equal length, not a longer one.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student picks a shorter length, suggesting confusion between more and less.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw two lines side by side and point to which extends further; stretch: ask the student to draw any line longer than 6 cm and state its approximate length.

exercise.description: Draw a string longer than the string given below.

items.prompt: Look at the decoration string below. It is 8 cm long. Which of the following is a string that is shorter than the decoration string?

options.label: A
options.text: A string that is 10 cm long.

options.label: B
options.text: A string that is 12 cm long.

options.label: C
options.text: A string that is 5 cm long.

options.label: D
options.text: A string that is 8 cm long.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: D — a string that is 5 cm long is shorter than 8 cm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare the numbers: any length less than 8 cm is shorter than the given decoration string.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student picks a longer string, confusing 'shorter' with 'longer'.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student picks an equal-length string, not a shorter one.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student picks a length even longer than A, suggesting 'shorter' has not been understood.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: lay two pieces of string side by side with one end aligned and point to which ends first; stretch: name the lengths in order from shortest to longest and identify which are shorter than 8 cm.

exercise.description: Draw a string shorter than the decoration string Shelly and Adi are holding.

items.prompt: A rectangular board has a border. Each side of the border can hold 3 unit strings. The board has 4 sides. How many unit strings are needed to cover the entire border?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply the number of unit strings per side by the number of sides: 3 × 4 = 12.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw the four sides of the board and place 3 marks on each side, then count all marks; stretch: ask how many unit strings would be needed if each side held 4 strings instead of 3.

exercise.description: How many of the given unit-string are needed to decorate the entire border of the board?

items.section_title: Measuring with metre, half metre, and quarter metre
items.prompt: Sona has a rope that is one metre long. She wants to cut it into equal pieces so that each piece is a quarter metre long. How many cuts does she need to make?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 3 cuts. One metre divided into 4 equal quarter-metre pieces requires 3 cuts.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Fold the one-metre rope into 4 equal parts; the number of cuts is always one less than the number of pieces: 4 − 1 = 3.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: fold a strip of paper into 4 parts and count the fold lines (which become the cut lines); stretch: ask how many cuts would be needed to make 8 equal pieces from the same rope.

exercise.description: Cut a one-metre rope into 4 equal pieces. How many cuts did you make?
